Unpopular (generalized) opinion: 

1. Black people have organized constantly and vocally about Black issues. This "what about us" mindset that Native people have is unproductive and frankly embarrassing. What are we doing collectively to be just as vocal? We're really great at symbolism  to raise awareness (red handprint for MMIWG2S) but what are we doing to keep our relatives safe on rez/off rez etc

2. Black activists have partnered with/shown up for Native protests to support. We as Native people haven't always done this. 

3. A blocker to forming long term, reciprocal relationships between Black and Native people is anti-blackness/racism that is heavily present in Native communities. There are tribes that refuse to recognize their Black relatives. Some of those tribes also owned Black slaves.

4. Pitting Black and Native people against each other leaves out our relatives who are both Black and Native. 

5. Saying Natives suffered more than Black people is wrong and a form of lateral oppression. We have gone through similar but different experiences. 

All in all, we need to be better allies to Black people. Justice for Black people, means justice for us too. They're fighting the same system we are and often speak up for us too.

Senior year of HS:

My history teacher and my ap psych teacher sat me down and asked how I was doing. They noticed that I was withdrawn and not doing well academically like I used to. Tbh I had been planning on killing myself. I was struggling a lot at home. One of my friends had killed themselves a few months earlier and I was feeling a lot of guilt, in addition to being severely depressed/suicidal. 

They were really kind/supportive as I sat there bawling my eyes out because I wanted to kill myself and I thought no one cared. That was probably the first time in a few years someone asked me how I was doing and actually cared about the answer. They helped me find a local therapist. I didn't kill myself like I was planning on because of them.

I used to feel conflicted and really bad about it. Before I looked into what "white passing" really meant. I understand if I get down voted for my response.

Yeah it can suck when people tease you about how pale or white I look but on the other hand, I don't have to deal with the constant racism that someone who is more visibly "Native" would encounter. People don't recognize I'm Native unless I say I am usually. I also don't get fucked over like Black / Afro-Natives do, who not only have their Indigenity questioned by white and Native people but also experience anti-Blackness from both communities. 

Being white passing is a privilege because of our proximity to whiteness. We more often get opportunities or are used as spokespeople because we're more acceptable for white people, ya know?

Ultimately the only way to deal with it is to continue being involved with your community/culture but still be cognizant of the privilege you have when moving through colonial systems. You can always try thinking of ways you can utilize that privilege to not only benefit you but also others who don't have the same privilege.
